title: New Year's Hangover: How to Drink on NYE and Recover Jan 1
excerpt: Why New Year's Eve hangovers hit so hard, an hour-by-hour plan for drinking on NYE without wrecking January 1, what actually helps the morning after, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Why New Year's Eve hangovers hit so hard, an hour-by-hour plan for the night, what helps on New Year's Day, and the warning signs that need real help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** New Year's Eve hangovers tend to be worse than an ordinary night out, and it isn't bad luck. It's the combination of drinking for more hours than usual, mixing drinks, bubbly champagne at midnight, snacking instead of eating, and getting to bed at 2 or 3 a.m. Nothing you can buy cancels that out. What does work is a plan for the night itself: eat a real dinner, pace yourself, sip water between drinks, go easy on the midnight toast, and sort out your ride home before you leave. This guide walks through why New Year's Eve drinking hits so hard, a simple hour-by-hour plan, what to do on New Year's Day if you wake up feeling rough, and the warning signs that mean someone needs real help.

**The quick rules:** Eat a full meal before your first drink. Pick your number of drinks before you go out. Alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water. Stick to one or two drink types. Sip the midnight champagne rather than refilling it. Stop drinking about an hour or two before you plan to sleep. Never drive, and book or plan a ride home in advance, because rides are scarce and expensive after midnight.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article shares general guidance for adults who drink socially. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if** someone can't be woken up, is confused or very disoriented, is vomiting while barely conscious, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long gaps between breaths), has a seizure, or has pale, blue-tinged, or cold, clammy skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and it's an emergency. Don't leave them to "sleep it off." Turn them on their side and stay with them until help arrives. **See a doctor the next day if** you can't keep fluids down, have severe stomach pain, notice blood in vomit or stool, have a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, or still feel confused. And if you find you get the shakes, heavy sweating, or anxiety that only eases with another drink, tell a doctor. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical issue worth getting checked, not a hangover quirk.

## Why New Year's Eve Drinking Hits Harder Than a Normal Night Out

Most people don't drink dramatically more on New Year's Eve than at any other party. What changes is everything around the drinking. Here's what stacks up.

### It's a long night

A typical Friday out might be a few drinks over three or four hours. New Year's Eve often starts with drinks at dinner around 7 or 8 p.m. and runs past 1 a.m. More hours usually means more drinks, and it also means your body is processing alcohol for a long stretch without a break. The liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults (it varies a lot from person to person), and there's nothing you can do to speed it up. If you keep drinking faster than that, the alcohol in your blood keeps climbing all night.

### The midnight champagne lands on top of everything else

The toast at midnight usually comes after several hours of drinking, not instead of it. That glass or two of bubbly goes on top of whatever you've already had. There's also some evidence that carbonation matters: a small UK study comparing flat and sparkling champagne found that people's blood alcohol rose faster with the bubbly version. The effect varies between people, but it fits with what many notice, which is that sparkling drinks seem to hit quickly. We cover this in more detail in our [champagne hangover guide](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

### People mix drinks

Cocktails before dinner, wine with the meal, shots at a party, champagne at midnight. The old rhyme about "beer before liquor" doesn't hold up well in research. What matters most is the total amount of alcohol, not the order. But mixing drinks makes it much harder to keep count, and some drinks carry more congeners, the byproducts of fermentation and aging found in larger amounts in darker drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine. Studies comparing bourbon and vodka have found that people tend to report worse hangovers after the bourbon at the same blood alcohol level. Switching between drink types also tends to come with a few "just one more" extras.

### Party snacks instead of a meal

Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol passes into your bloodstream. A plate of canapés and a handful of chips spread over five hours doesn't do much. People heading out early also sometimes skip dinner to "save room" or because they're getting ready, which is about the worst setup for a long night.

### Short, broken sleep

This is the part people underestimate. Alcohol already makes sleep worse. It can help you nod off, but it disrupts the second half of the night, cuts into REM sleep, and wakes you up early, often around 4 or 5 a.m. Now add a bedtime of 2 or 3 a.m. and maybe a noisy house or a couch at a friend's place. A short, broken night on its own leaves you tired, foggy, and irritable. Researchers who study hangovers consistently point to poor sleep as one of the things that makes hangovers feel worse. If you've ever lain awake at dawn after a big night, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.

### Cold weather and crowds

If you're out at a fireworks display or walking between parties in winter, it's worth knowing that alcohol makes you feel warmer than you are. It widens the blood vessels near your skin, which gives a warm flush but actually lets your body lose heat faster. Add standing outside at midnight in light party clothes, and you can get colder than you realize. Crowds also mean long waits for bathrooms and bars, which can lead to ordering two drinks at a time to "save a trip."

## How Much Are You Actually Drinking? A Quick Standard-Drink Check

It's easy to lose count on New Year's Eve because glasses get topped up and drinks come in all sizes. In the US, one standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

| Drink | Approximate size of one standard drink |
|---|---|
| Beer (about 5% alcohol) | 12 oz (one regular can or bottle) |
| Wine or champagne (about 12% alcohol) | 5 oz (a standard glass, smaller than many party pours) |
| Spirits (about 40% alcohol) | 1.5 oz (one shot) |

A few things that catch people out:

- **A 750 ml bottle of champagne or wine holds about five standard drinks.** Splitting one between two people means about two and a half each, before anything else.
- **Cocktails are often more than one drink.** Many mixed drinks contain two shots or more, and sweet mixers make them easy to finish fast.
- **Topped-up glasses don't feel like new drinks.** If someone keeps refilling your glass, you can drink a whole bottle without ever "finishing" a glass.

## How to Not Get a Hangover on New Year's Eve: An Hour-by-Hour Plan

No plan guarantees zero hangover if you drink a lot. The goal is fewer drinks spread over more time, with food, water, and as much sleep as you can manage. Here's a simple framework you can adjust to your own night.

### The day of New Year's Eve

- **Drink water through the day.** You don't need to "pre-hydrate" with gallons, but starting the night already thirsty doesn't help.
- **Eat properly.** A good lunch and a real dinner before drinking. Meals with protein, some fat, and fiber slow how quickly alcohol reaches your blood. Think pasta with meat sauce, a burrito, salmon and rice, rather than a light salad.
- **Grab a nap if you can.** Since you'll be up late, an afternoon nap is one of the easiest ways to offset some of the lost sleep.
- **Plan your ride home now.** Decide who's driving (and not drinking), book a car service, check transit hours, or arrange to stay over. Rides after midnight are in short supply and surge pricing is common, so a plan made sober is much better than one made at 1 a.m.
- **Set your number.** Decide how many drinks you'll have and roughly when. It's much easier to stick to a limit you chose in advance.

### 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.: the early evening

- **Start slow.** The first couple of hours are where many people get ahead of themselves. One drink per hour is a reasonable pace.
- **Alternate every drink with water or soda water.** This is the single most useful habit. It slows you down, gives your hands something to hold, and helps with thirst.
- **Pick one or two drink types.** Lighter drinks like vodka, gin, and white wine tend to have fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy, and red wine. Keeping to one or two types also makes counting easier.
- **Watch out for big cocktails and punches.** Punch bowls are a classic New Year's trap. You have no idea how strong they are.

### 10 p.m. to midnight: the build-up

- **Eat again.** If there's real food at the party, have some. If not, a late snack still helps a little.
- **Skip the shots.** Shots taken in a row raise your blood alcohol fast, and that spike is when people make the decisions they regret.
- **Keep the water going.** It's easy to drop the water habit once the party gets going.
- **Save room for the toast.** If champagne at midnight matters to you, have a glass of water or a soft drink right before so you're not drinking it on top of a fresh cocktail.

### Midnight: the toast

- **One glass, sipped.** You don't need to drain it to celebrate. Hold it, toast, enjoy it slowly.
- **Say no to automatic refills.** Put your hand over the glass or keep it half full. People pouring champagne at midnight are rarely counting.
- **Don't go hard on cheap bubbly.** Sweet, inexpensive sparkling wine is easy to drink fast. Whatever you're drinking, the amount matters far more than the price.

### After midnight: winding down

- **Switch to water or soft drinks.** For many people, the hour after midnight is the most useful time to stop. You've had the celebration. Everything after this is mostly adding to tomorrow.
- **Stop an hour or two before bed.** This gives your body a bit of time to start catching up before you try to sleep.
- **Eat something small before leaving** if you're hungry.
- **Get home the way you planned.** Never drive after drinking, and don't get in a car with someone who has been drinking. Stay with your friends and make sure everyone has a way home.

### Before bed

- **Drink a glass of water** and leave another by the bed.
- **Take off contacts, wash your face, and charge your phone.** Small things that make the morning easier.
- **Don't take Tylenol "just in case."** Taking acetaminophen while alcohol is still being processed adds work for your liver, and it won't prevent a hangover. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Clear your morning.** If you can, give yourself a slow start on New Year's Day instead of an early alarm.

For a broader look at drinking through the whole season, see our [holiday drinking survival guide](/never-hungover/holiday-drinking-survival-guide-health-first-approach). And if you're hosting or going to a party where you know the drinking will be heavy, our [pre-game party strategy](/never-hungover/pre-game-party-strategy-dhm-2025) covers more tactics.

## The Champagne Question: Is Bubbly Really Worse?

Champagne and other sparkling wines get blamed for a lot of New Year's Day pain. Some of that is fair, some isn't.

**What's fair:**

- **Bubbles may speed things up.** As mentioned above, there's small-study evidence that carbonated drinks can raise blood alcohol faster than flat ones, at least for some people. A faster rise can mean you feel drunk sooner and are more likely to keep going.
- **It's easy to lose count.** Flutes are small, they get refilled constantly, and bottles get passed around.
- **It's drunk late.** By midnight, most people have already had several drinks, so the champagne pushes the total over the edge.

**What's overblown:**

- **Champagne isn't a "dirty" drink.** It's not especially high in congeners compared with dark spirits. A glass of champagne contains about the same alcohol as a glass of white wine.
- **Price isn't magic.** Expensive champagne won't spare you if you drink a lot of it, and cheap sparkling wine won't hurt you more at the same amount. Some people do find very sweet drinks easier to overdo, though.
- **Sulfites are rarely the cause.** Wine does contain sulfites, but true sulfite sensitivity is uncommon, and it usually shows up as breathing or skin symptoms rather than a headache the next day.

The practical fix is simple: have it, enjoy it, sip it, and don't let it be the fourth or fifth drink stacked on everything else.

## New Year's Day Hangover: What Actually Helps

If you wake up on January 1 feeling rough, here's what's worth doing and what's not. The honest truth is that time is the main cure. Most hangovers fade within about 24 hours. Everything else just makes the wait more bearable. A well-known systematic review in the BMJ looked at the research on hangover remedies and found no convincing evidence that any of them prevents or treats hangovers, and the picture hasn't changed much since.

### What's worth doing

- **Drink fluids steadily.** Water is fine. An electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution can help if you were sick or are very thirsty. Sip rather than chug, especially if your stomach is unsettled.
- **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, soup, or rice. Eggs and toast are a classic for a reason: they're easy on the stomach and give you some protein and carbs.
- **Take a pain reliever carefully if you need one.** A single standard dose of ibuprofen with food is a common choice for a headache. Skip it if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or take blood thinners. Be careful with acetaminophen after a heavy night, and never stack products that contain it, like cold and flu medicines.
- **Rest.** Go back to sleep if you can. A nap in the afternoon helps too.
- **Get some fresh air and light.** A short, easy walk can make you feel more alert, and daylight helps reset your body clock after a late night.
- **Have some coffee if you normally do.** If you're a regular coffee drinker, skipping it can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of your hangover. Just don't use it in place of water.

### What's not worth doing

- **Hair of the dog.** A drink in the morning can dull symptoms for a while because you're adding alcohol back, but it just pushes the hangover later and keeps your body processing alcohol. There's no good evidence it helps.
- **Greasy food as a "cure."** A big fry-up the morning after might be comforting, but it doesn't soak up alcohol that's already in your blood. Food helps most before and during drinking, not after.
- **Hard exercise to "sweat it out."** Alcohol is cleared mainly by your liver, not your sweat. A punishing workout when you're dehydrated and short on sleep can make you feel worse. Gentle movement is fine.
- **Viral cures and IV drips.** Pickle juice, exotic teas, and the latest social media trend mostly lack good evidence. IV hydration services do give you fluids, but most people with a normal hangover can rehydrate by drinking.
- **Driving early.** If you drank heavily late into the night, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning. If you finished drinking at 2 a.m. after a long night, it's not safe to assume you're fine to drive at 8 a.m.

If your main symptoms are trembling hands or feeling shaky, see our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes). If the next morning comes with dread and anxiety, that's common too, and our guide on [hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why it happens.

## How Long Does a New Year's Hangover Last?

Hangovers usually start as your blood alcohol falls and tend to be worst around the time it reaches zero. After a night that ended at 1 or 2 a.m., that often means feeling worst from mid-morning into the early afternoon. For most people, symptoms fade by the evening or within about 24 hours of the last drink.

Things that tend to make it last longer:

- A very large total amount of alcohol
- Very little sleep
- Being sick or getting dehydrated
- Not eating the day after
- Darker drinks with more congeners

If you still feel very unwell more than a day later, can't keep fluids down, or are confused, that's no longer a normal hangover, and it's worth getting medical advice.

## Staying Safe on New Year's Eve

New Year's Eve is one of the busiest nights of the year for emergency rooms and for drunk-driving crashes. A few simple habits go a long way.

### Getting home

- **Plan your ride before you start drinking.** A designated sober driver, a booked car, public transit, or staying over.
- **Never drive after drinking**, even if you "feel fine." Alcohol affects judgment and reaction time before you notice it.
- **Don't let friends drive** after drinking. Take keys if you need to.
- **Stick together.** Make sure everyone in your group has a way home and that nobody leaves alone and very drunk.

### Looking out for friends: signs of alcohol poisoning

This is important enough to repeat. Alcohol poisoning happens when someone drinks so much that the parts of the brain controlling breathing, heart rate, and temperature start to shut down. On a big night, it can happen to anyone, especially with shots and drinking games.

**Call 911 right away if someone:**

- Can't be woken up, or won't respond to you
- Is confused or very disoriented
- Is vomiting while drowsy or semi-conscious
- Has slow breathing or long gaps between breaths
- Has a seizure
- Has pale, bluish, or cold, clammy skin, or a very low body temperature

While you wait, keep them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or more food or drink. These don't help and can make things worse. Most US states have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan rules that offer some protection to people who call for help in an alcohol emergency, but rules vary. Calling is always the right thing to do.

### Drinking games and shots

Drinking games and rounds of shots are the most common way a fun night turns into a dangerous one. They push you to drink faster than your body can keep up with. If you play, swap in water or a soft drink for some rounds, or keep score in some other way.

## Should You Plan for a Dry January?

Lots of people use New Year's Day as a starting point for a month off alcohol or cutting back. If a rough January 1 has you thinking about it, it can be a good reset: many people notice better sleep, more energy, and a clearer head within a few weeks. You don't have to go all in. Cutting back to fewer drinking days, or setting a firm weekly limit, is also a reasonable goal.

If you drink heavily every day and stopping suddenly gives you shakes, sweats, anxiety, or trouble sleeping, talk to a doctor before quitting. Stopping heavy daily drinking abruptly can cause withdrawal, which can be serious and is best handled with medical support.

## What About Supplements for New Year's Eve?

You'll see plenty of "hangover cure" products advertised around the holidays. It's worth being clear about what the evidence does and doesn't show.

- **There is no good evidence that any supplement prevents a hangover.** Eating, pacing, water, and sleep do far more than anything in a bottle.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, and human data are limited. Some people like to take it before a big night as part of their routine. It doesn't make it safe to drink more, and it doesn't lower your blood alcohol for driving. If you want to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly pick, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare brands.
- **Electrolyte drinks** can help with rehydration the next day, especially if you were sick, but they don't stop a hangover on their own.
- **Check with a doctor or pharmacist first** if you take any regular medications, are pregnant, or have liver or kidney problems.

Whatever you choose, treat it as an extra, not a plan. Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.

## The Bottom Line

- New Year's Eve hangovers are usually worse because of a long night, mixed drinks, midnight champagne, little real food, and short, broken sleep.
- The most effective plan is simple: eat a proper dinner, set a number, alternate with water, sip the midnight toast, stop well before bed, and plan your ride home.
- On New Year's Day, fluids, gentle food, rest, and careful use of a pain reliever help you get through it. Time is what actually ends a hangover.
- There is no good evidence that hair of the dog, greasy breakfasts, or supplements cure a hangover.
- If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, has a seizure, or has cold, bluish skin, call 911. Don't let them sleep it off.

**Related reading:** [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking), [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas), [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you avoid a hangover on New Year's Eve?**

The only reliable way is to drink less, so the useful question is how to drink less without feeling like you're missing out. Eat a real dinner before you start, decide on a number of drinks in advance, alternate every drink with a glass of water, sip the midnight champagne instead of refilling it, and stop drinking about an hour or two before you plan to sleep. Get home safely and drink water before bed. There is no good evidence that any pill or supplement prevents a hangover on its own.

**Why do New Year's Eve hangovers feel so much worse than normal?**

Several things stack up on one night. People drink for longer than usual, often from early evening to past 1 a.m., mix drink types, have bubbly drinks that can be absorbed faster, eat less because they're snacking at a party, and get far less sleep than normal. Short, broken sleep on its own makes you feel tired, foggy, and irritable, and it adds to everything alcohol is already doing.

**Does champagne give you a worse hangover?**

Champagne itself isn't uniquely toxic, but it has a few traits that make it easy to overdo. The bubbles may help alcohol reach your blood a little faster, the glasses get topped up so you lose count, and it's usually drunk on top of whatever else you had that night. A full 750 ml bottle at about 12% alcohol contains roughly five US standard drinks, so a bottle shared between two people adds up quickly.

**What is the best thing to do for a hangover on New Year's Day?**

Drink water or an electrolyte drink steadily, eat something easy like toast, eggs, or soup, and rest. If you have a headache, a single standard dose of ibuprofen with food is usually a better choice than stacking acetaminophen (Tylenol) the morning after heavy drinking, unless you have stomach or kidney problems. Fresh air and a short walk can help you feel more human. Time is what actually ends a hangover, and most are gone within 24 hours.

**Does 'hair of the dog' work on New Year's Day?**

There's no good evidence that it helps. A morning drink can dull symptoms for a short while because you're adding alcohol back, but it delays recovery and keeps your body processing alcohol for longer. If you feel you need a drink to stop shaking or feel normal, that's a sign to talk to a doctor rather than a hangover tip.

**How long does a New Year's hangover last?**

Most hangovers peak around the time your blood alcohol returns to zero, often mid-morning to early afternoon after a late night, and fade within about 24 hours. A very heavy night, little sleep, or dehydration can stretch that out. If you still feel very unwell, can't keep fluids down, or are confused the next day, it's no longer a normal hangover and you should get medical advice.

**Is it safe to sleep it off after a heavy New Year's Eve?**

For someone who is drowsy but awake, talking, and breathing normally, yes, with a glass of water nearby and lying on their side. It is not safe to leave someone to sleep it off if they can't be woken, are confused, are vomiting while barely conscious, have slow or irregular breathing, have seizures, or have pale, blue-tinged, or cold skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and you should call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

**Can DHM stop a New Year's Eve hangover?**

There is no good evidence that DHM stops hangovers in people. It's a plant compound with interesting early research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal and lab studies with very little human data. Some people like to take it before a big night, but it doesn't replace eating, pacing, water, and sleep, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more or to drive.
